description: I’m a PhD student and a machine learning and data engineer. My interests include hydrology, Earth observation, and data visualization. I'm participating solo in the São Gonçalo local event
summary:
RainShift is a web tool that lets anyone check whether rainfall and air temperature have really changed on the northern coast of Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, from the Macaé River headwaters to Campos dos Goytacazes. It takes two NASA records, GPM IMERG precipitation and MERRA-2 air temperature, and shows for the whole region and for every grid cell what changed, where, by how much, and how strong the statistical evidence is.

The problem it addresses is that a trend line is easy to draw and easy to over-read. RainShift reports every trend with its 95% confidence interval drawn against zero and gives one of three plain labels: increase, decrease, or insufficient evidence of a trend. With real data the two variables tell different stories. The region warmed by about 0.22 °C per decade (95% CI 0.12 to 0.32), close to 1 °C in 45 years. Rainfall shows an estimated decline of 76 mm per decade, but the interval runs from −218 to +76, so 26 years of data cannot tell a decline from no change, and the estimate nearly doubles if the record starts in 2001 instead of 1999.

This matters because students, teachers and people who manage water in the region need to know not only what the data suggest but how far the data can be trusted. Four guided cases, a period selector that recomputes the trend live, and a plain-language glossary turn a statistics lesson into a detective exercise on real NASA data.
details:
What exactly does it do?

  • Shows a full-screen map of grid cells coloured by the estimated trend, and a time series with its trend line for the region average or any cell you click.
  • Covers two variables with four yearly metrics each. Precipitation: annual, wet-season and dry-season totals, and the wet-season share. Air temperature: annual, wet-season and dry-season means, and the wet-minus-dry contrast.
  • For every series, reports the trend per decade, the 95% confidence interval, the number of years, the period, the source and the unit, and one label: Increase, Decrease, or Insufficient evidence of a trend.
  • Lets you change the start and end year and recomputes the trend in the browser, so you can see how much an answer depends on the years chosen.
  • Offers four guided cases that set the controls and explain what to look at: "Getting warmer?", "Less rain?", "Does the start year matter?" and "Do the seasons differ?".
  • Includes a glossary, a one-sentence reading "in plain words" for every result, and CSV download of every series.

How does it work?

  • A Python pipeline downloads bounding-box subsets from NASA GES DISC through Harmony, checks units, coordinates, dates and missing values, and converts the monthly values (rain rate in mm/hr × hours in the month; temperature in K to °C).
  • The region average weights each cell by the geodesic area that lies inside the region.
  • The wet season is defined from the rainfall record itself (the run of months rainier than the average month: November to March). Years run from November to October so that a wet season is never split in two.
  • Trends use the Theil–Sen slope with Sen's 95% confidence interval and the Mann–Kendall test, with the Hamed–Rao correction when neighbouring years resemble each other. The map applies a Benjamini–Hochberg correction for testing many cells at once and is labelled exploratory.
  • The pipeline writes small JSON and GeoJSON files. The website is static: it needs no server and no NASA login, so it keeps working during judging.

What did we find?

  • Air temperature (MERRA-2, 1981–2025): +0.22 °C per decade, 95% CI +0.12 to +0.32. All 16 cells pass the many-tests correction. Both seasons warmed, but the data cannot tell whether one warms faster than the other: the wet-minus-dry contrast is −0.10 °C per decade, CI −0.25 to +0.04.
  • Precipitation (IMERG, 1999–2024): −76 mm per decade, 95% CI −218 to +76. None of the 204 cells passes the correction for the annual total. Starting the record in 2001 changes the estimate to −133 mm per decade, with the same label.
  • Two "significant" labels are not a comparison. To test whether seasons differ, RainShift fits the trend of the paired difference instead of comparing labels.

What benefits does it have?

  • It teaches how a trend is estimated and tested, with a real case where the answer is clear and a real case where it is not.
  • It keeps two things apart that are often mixed up: statistical uncertainty (how much the values jump from year to year) and the limits of the data products themselves.
  • Every series can be downloaded as CSV from the app, and the method page documents each step, so the numbers can be checked independently.

What do we hope to achieve?

A tool that classrooms and local water and climate groups can use to ask "has the climate here really changed?" and get an honest answer, and a pipeline that can be pointed at other regions and other NASA variables.

Limits

  • The region is a rectangular box aligned to the IMERG grid, not a watershed boundary.
  • IMERG is a merged satellite and rain-gauge estimate; MERRA-2 is a model reconstruction on cells of about 55 × 65 km that mix land, mountains and ocean.
  • The confidence interval covers year-to-year variability only. Trends are linear; the rainfall series looks more like a rise followed by a fall.
  • The period selector uses the same estimator in the browser without the Hamed–Rao correction and shows a caution note when it would matter.

Tools, languages and software

A Python pipeline for the data and the statistics, and a static website built with Next.js, React and CesiumJS. The project is licensed under Apache-2.0.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes. An SI/AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Anthropic) was used throughout:

  • Planning: it helped turn the idea into a technical plan and checked the official rules and data catalogues.
  • Code: it wrote most of the Python pipeline, the tests and the web application, under the author's direction and review.

The project idea, the research question, the choice of region, data and methods, and all decisions were made by the author. No images, video or audio were generated with SI. No data values were generated: every number comes from the NASA products listed below. SI use is acknowledged in the application's "Method & credits" page, in the metadata file published with each dataset (`meta.json`, field `si_note`) and in the project's source files.

NASA Data

  • GPM IMERG Final Precipitation L3 1 month 0.1 degree x 0.1 degree V07 (GPM_3IMERGM), NASA GES DISC. DOI: 10.5067/GPM/IMERG/3B-MONTH/07. Variable `precipitation`, January 1998 to September 2025, 204 grid cells. Used for all rainfall series, maps and for defining the wet season.
  • MERRA-2 tavgM_2d_slv_Nx, monthly mean single-level diagnostics V5.12.4 (M2TMNXSLV), NASA GMAO / GES DISC. DOI: 10.5067/AP1B0BA5PD2K. Variable `T2M` (2-metre air temperature), January 1980 to September 2026, 16 grid cells. Used for all temperature series and maps.
  • NASA Earthdata Login, Harmony and the Common Metadata Repository (CMR): used to find the collections and to download bounding-box subsets.
  • NASA `earthaccess` and `harmony-py` Python libraries: used for authentication and downloads.

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References

No Space Agency Partner data were used.

  • OpenStreetMap map tiles, OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL: base map, loaded at view time.
  • CesiumJS: map engine.
  • NASA earthaccess and harmony-py: data access.
  • Open-source software: Python scientific libraries (xarray, SciPy, pymannkendall, statsmodels) for the analysis; Next.js, React and Recharts for the website.

Methods

  • Sen, P. K. (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall's tau. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 63(324), 1379–1389.
  • Mann, H. B. (1945). Nonparametric tests against trend. Econometrica, 13(3), 245–259.
  • Hamed, K. H., & Rao, A. R. (1998). A modified Mann–Kendall trend test for autocorrelated data. Journal of Hydrology, 204(1–4), 182–196.
  • Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 57(1), 289–300.
